povertyAndFaith: Home Monkey Blog · Data Dossier · Dossier de Dados English Português Politics, Law & Justice · Data Dossier The Poor and the Faithful A serious answer to a question many people carry silently: is it my impression, or is poverty in Muslim countries less harsh and less radical than in Christian countries? The honest answer needs numbers, real examples on both sides, and one distinction that almost every argument about this skips. Poverty Religion & data Welfare Muslim-majority countries Christian-majority countries Bilingual 1. The claim, stated properly The question, as it is usually asked in Portuguese, runs like this: «Será impressão minha ou nos países muçulmanos a pobreza não chega a ser tão dura e tão radical, quanto aos países cristãos?» — is it my impression, or in Muslim countries does poverty not become as hard and as radical as in Christian countries? It deserves a straight answer, because the question underneath it is legitimate even when its framing is not: people notice that the poorest places they hear about in the news are often Christian-majority (Haiti, the favelas of Brazil, the street homeless of Los Angeles) and that the Muslim-majority countries they see in images look organised, hospitable and often rich (Doha, Dubai, Istanbul). Both observations are real. Neither one is evidence. Three clarifications before the data, because they decide everything that follows. An impression measures visibility, not poverty. What you can see is filtered by press freedom, by whether begging is tolerated in public, by where tourists are taken, and by which disasters get cameras. Extreme rural poverty in the Sahel, in Afghanistan or in Bangladesh is far less photogenic than a tent on a Los Angeles pavement. "Muslim countries" and "Christian countries" are not comparable units. There are around fifty Muslim-majority states, several of them among the richest on earth per person and several among the poorest. Christianity is the majority religion in roughly half the planet's countries — Norway, Haiti, the Philippines, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United States are all in the same group. Any average across such a group hides more than it shows. Poverty is not a religion and religion is not an income. The measurable drivers of destitution are the ones the World Bank, the UN and national statistical offices keep testing: state capacity, conflict, growth, the distribution of land and oil rents, education, health systems, jobs and social transfers. Religion can shape some of those — through charity institutions, family norms, law — but it is not the variable that does most of the work, and no dataset has ever shown that it is. So this dossier does three things: it gives the numbers for both groups, it takes the part of the question that is defensible and shows exactly what produces it, and it names the part that is not defensible. It is not an attack on the question. It is an attempt to answer it better than it was asked. 2. How poverty is measured, and why that decides the answer Almost every dispute about "which poverty is worse" is really a dispute about the instrument. There are four instruments in common use, and each one is honest about something different. The international poverty line. The World Bank anchors it to the national poverty lines of the poorest countries. In June 2025 it was updated to $3.00 per person per day (2021 prices), replacing the old $2.15 line. It measures whether a household can buy a survival basket of food and essentials. It says nothing about dignity, debt, housing quality or safety. The multidimensional poverty index (MPI). Built by UNDP and OPHI, it counts deprivations in health, education and living standards — nutrition, child mortality, years of schooling, school attendance, cooking fuel, sanitation, water, electricity, housing, assets. It catches the poverty that a market basket misses, and it is the measure in which "poverty is harsh" is most visible. National poverty lines. Each country's own threshold. Useful for trend, useless for comparison: the Philippines' 15.5 per cent in 2023 and Yemen's 74 per cent in 2022 are not measuring the same basket of goods. Relative poverty , used by the OECD (below half the median income of the country). This is the measure that shows poverty in rich countries — the reason Israel can record 21 per cent poor in 2024 and the United States 10.6 per cent in 2024 while Yemen records 74 per cent. The consequence is blunt: a Christian-majority country with a weak welfare state and high inequality will look poor on the relative measure and fine on the absolute one; a Muslim-majority rentier state with oil money and a tiny citizen population will look rich on both while holding hundreds of thousands of migrant workers outside its social contract entirely. If the question uses "poor" to mean "living on very little money" the answer comes from the first two instruments. If it uses "poor" to mean "falling behind the neighbours you can see", it comes from the fourth, and then the comparison is between welfare states. The same two countries can swap places depending on which line you draw. That is not a scandal about the data; it is the reason any honest answer has to name its measure out loud. 3. The numbers, side by side Three global facts frame everything below. In 2026, about 811 million people — one in ten — live on less than $3.00 a day , a rate essentially unchanged since 2019; more than half of the world's extreme poor live in just nine economies ; and by 2030 about 87 per cent are projected to live in Sub-Saharan Africa or in fragile and conflict-affected states. On the multidimensional measure, 1.2 billion people out of 6.3 billion (18.9 per cent) in 108 countries are in acute multidimensional poverty — the first rise since the index began in 2010 — with 616 million of them in Sub-Saharan Africa (51.4 per cent of its population); more than half of all the multidimensionally poor are children, and eight in ten live in rural areas. The table is a selection of real, documented cases, not a ranking. The filter below the caption switches between the groups. Group All Muslim-majority Christian-majority Neither 15 / 15 Poverty, measured — selected countries, with the instrument and the year Country Majority Measure Latest figure Year Yemen Muslim Multidimensional poverty (UNDP) 82.7 % 2024 Yemen Muslim National poverty line (World Bank) 74 % 2022 Afghanistan Muslim Unable to meet basic needs (UNDP) 74 % — three in four 2025 Gaza (Palestine) Muslim Population below the poverty line (UNCTAD) 100 % — 2.3 million 2025 Nigeria Muslim / Christian Multidimensional poverty (NBS) 63 % — 133 million 2022 Indonesia Muslim Health insurance coverage, JKN 280 million — 98 % 2025 Qatar, the UAE Muslim Income per person (World Bank) about $30,000 to $80,000 a year 2023 DR Congo Christian National poverty line (INS / World Bank) 69 % 2024 Ethiopia Christian Poverty rate, rising again (World Bank) 43 % 2025 Ethiopia Christian Multidimensional poverty 72 % 2024 Haiti Christian Poorest country in the Western Hemisphere (World Bank) 1.5 million displaced 2026 Philippines Christian Official poverty incidence (PSA) 15.5 % — 17.5 million 2023 United States Christian Official poverty rate (Census Bureau) 10.6 % — 35.9 million 2024 Israel Jewish Poverty, national insurance report 21 % — 2 million 2024 India Hindu The $3.00 line, over a decade 27.1 % → 5.3 % 2011 → 2023 Read the table twice. In the first four rows a Muslim-majority country shows some of the harshest poverty recorded anywhere on earth: three quarters of Yemen and of Afghanistan, and the entire population of Gaza. In the next rows another Muslim-majority country shows the opposite extreme, and a fifth — Indonesia — has built a health insurer covering 98 per cent of its population. On the Christian side the same spread appears: the Democratic Republic of the Congo at 69 per cent and Ethiopia at 43 per cent against the United States at 10.6 per cent, with Haiti at the bottom of its hemisphere. And the single largest poverty reduction in the table, India's, happened in a Hindu-majority country. 4. The finding: the difference inside each group is bigger than the difference between them Take the two groups as people usually mean them. Inside the Muslim-majority group, income per person runs from roughly a few hundred dollars a year in Afghanistan to above thirty thousand in Saudi Arabia and above eighty thousand in Qatar: a factor of two hundred between two states that share the same majority religion and, in some cases, the same legal tradition. Inside the Christian-majority group the same spread appears: Norway, Denmark and Switzerland at the top of every human-development table, the Democratic Republic of the Congo at 69 per cent below the national poverty line and Haiti the poorest country in its hemisphere. That spread is the whole answer to the original question, and it is not a rhetorical trick. It is what the World Bank's own data show when you stop averaging: poverty is not distributed by creed, it is distributed by geography, conflict and rent. In 2026 more than half of the world's extremely poor live in nine economies — a set that includes Muslim-majority, Hindu-majority and mixed states — and by 2030 about 87 per cent of them are projected to be in Sub-Saharan Africa or in fragile and conflict-affected situations. On the multidimensional measure, the deepest concentration on earth is Sub-Saharan Africa, with 616 million people (51.4 per cent) — a region that is roughly half Muslim and half Christian. Africa does not sort by religion. It sorts by war, by colonial borders, by commodity prices and by the capacity of a state to collect taxes and deliver services. Three consequences follow, and they are worth saying plainly. One Muslim-majority country cannot be compared with one Christian-majority country, and neither can the averages. With roughly fifty Muslim-majority states and about half the world's countries being Christian-majority, the groups contain both the richest societies ever measured and some of the poorest. The comparison people actually make is between subsets. In practice the eye compares the Gulf with Haiti, or Istanbul with a favela in Rio. Those are real photographs, but they are comparing the wealthiest corner of one group with the poorest corner of the other. The strongest correlates of destitution are known and boring: war, state capacity, dependence on a single commodity, tropical disease burden, isolation from markets, education, and whether women are permitted or able to work. The World Bank's 2026 assessment put a number on the last one: raising employment in poor households, including by closing the gender gap, would cut global extreme poverty by roughly a fifth. If the same religion produces both the richest and the poorest states in the file, then religion is not the variable doing the work. Something else is, and that something else is what this dossier is searching for. 5. Where the impression is half right — three real mechanisms There is a defensible version of the question, and it deserves real examples rather than a shrug. Three mechanisms genuinely soften the edge of poverty in specific Muslim-majority countries. None of them is the religion itself, and all three have Christian-majority equivalents or failures. A. Rent shared with citizens The Gulf states built their welfare on hydrocarbons: free or cheap energy and water, subsidised food, guaranteed public-sector jobs, no income tax, generous family allowances, and — after the price reforms — explicit cash compensation. Saudi Arabia's Citizen's Account , introduced with the 2018 round of energy reforms, was designed precisely to keep low- and middle-income households whole after the price rises; Iran did the same thing on a bigger scale in 2010, when it raised energy prices to market levels and paid a monthly transfer to almost every citizen (445,000 rials per person per month at the time), which economists still study as the largest such swap ever attempted. The result is real: some of the least visible poverty on earth, among citizens. The mechanism is the rent, not the faith. The proof is the rest of the class: Nigeria, Iraq, Angola, Libya and Algeria are oil states with mass poverty; Venezuela and Equatorial Guinea are oil states in other religious categories with the same result. Oil money makes a state generous to its own population when the population is small, and it does nothing of the kind when it is large or when the money is captured. B. Obligatory almsgiving and endowed charity as institutions Zakat is the most interesting of the three, because it has no exact Christian equivalent: it is a compulsory levy , commonly 2.5 per cent of qualifying wealth, and in several countries the state collects it. In Pakistan it is deducted at source from bank accounts; in Saudi Arabia, Malaysia and Sudan it is collected by official bodies; Indonesia has a national agency (BAZNAS) that reported around Rp 32.3 trillion collected in 2023 against an estimated national potential several times larger. Global estimates of annual zakat flows range from $200 billion to $1 trillion (a UNDP estimate quoted in the Islamic Development Bank's own materials) to $550–600 billion (a UN-ESCWA compilation). Even the lowest figure dwarfs global humanitarian aid. Historically the same logic ran through the waqf , the charitable endowment: hospitals, schools, fountains, soup kitchens and caravanserais financed by assets locked out of inheritance. Compare the instruments honestly: Christian charity has the tithe, the parish, the religious order and the relief agency — Caritas, the Salvation Army, the food banks — and these are voluntary or congregational, not a levy with state collection. That difference is real. What it produces, however, is not a gentler poverty but a different plumbing of relief. Egypt's Takaful and Karama transfers went from about 1 million households in 2018 to 4.5 million in 2025 ; Pakistan's BISP reaches many millions of households and is the country's largest social assistance programme; Indonesia's JKN health scheme covers 280 million people, about 98 per cent of the population . Those are state programmes funded by taxation and transfers as much as by alms, and they exist alongside zakat rather than instead of it. C. Family absorption, remittances and the taboo on visible begging The third mechanism is the household. In many Muslim-majority societies the informal obligation to feed a cousin, to host a relative, to send money home from the Gulf, is strong and enforceable through honour. Egypt, Pakistan and Bangladesh are among the world's largest recipients of worker remittances; a house in Kerala or a shop in Sylhet may be financed entirely by a brother abroad. Together with the norm that begging is shameful and should be handled privately or through the mosque, this produces something measurable and something optical at the same time. The measurable part is real relief to millions of people. The optical part is the point of this whole dossier: the same mechanism that genuinely softens some poverty also hides it. Poverty absorbed inside a family, a village or a mosque network does not appear on the pavement, so a foreign visitor does not see it. That is what produces the impression in the question, and it is also why the multidimensional index — which counts sanitation, schooling, fuel, nutrition, child mortality — repeatedly finds severe deprivation in countries whose streets look calm. One more equality, to keep the ledger straight: the world's most effective anti-poverty programmes of the last thirty years came mostly out of two traditions — the Nordic welfare state and the Latin American conditional cash transfer. Bolsa Família in Brazil, a Christian-majority country, kept 8.6 million people out of poverty between 2023 and 2024; without the social programmes, Brazil's extreme poverty rate would have been 10.0 per cent instead of 3.5 per cent. Mexico's Progresa-Oportunidades exported the model to dozens of countries. Bangladesh's BRAC exported its own: the Graduation approach, which lifts ultra-poor households out of destitution with assets, training and a stipend, and now runs in dozens of countries of every religion. 6. Where the impression breaks — the same countries, worst cases Now the other half of the same group. If the question were true as stated, the following situations should not exist. They do. Yemen. A Muslim-majority country in which 74 per cent of the population was below the national poverty line in 2022 (World Bank) and 82.7 per cent were multidimensionally poor in 2024 (UNDP). It is hard to find a harsher, more radical poverty on the planet, at any latitude. Afghanistan. Three out of four people unable to meet their basic needs in 2025, according to UNDP's own socioeconomic review — a figure that would have been called unthinkable in 2001. Gaza. UNCTAD's assessment in November 2025 found the economy collapsed by 83 per cent in 2024 and the entire population — 2.3 million people — below the poverty line. A UN report in July 2025 put poverty in Gaza near 100 per cent, up from 64 per cent before the war. The Sahel and the Horn. Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso, Chad and Somalia are Muslim-majority and among the poorest states in the world; the Sahel concentrates jihadist war, drought, displaced populations and state collapse. Somalia is routinely listed by World Bank-based compilations among the ten poorest countries on earth. South Asia. Bangladesh's programmes exist precisely because ultra-poverty there was extreme — people living on less than the cost of a minimum food basket, sleeping hungry, without assets. Pakistan's rural poverty and northern Nigeria's deprivation are of the same severity. The Gulf's own excluded class. This is the sharpest counterexample of all. In 2019 the ILO counted 24.1 million migrant workers in the Arab States , most of them in the Gulf, most of them from Muslim-majority countries themselves — Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Indonesia, Egypt, Ethiopia. They build the cities, clean the houses and dig the foundations, they are usually excluded from the welfare, the subsidies, the citizenship and often the labour law, and their status can depend on a single employer under the sponsorship system. A poverty that is real, but kept off the census and off the pavement. The pattern in that list is not religion. It is war and state failure (Yemen, Afghanistan, Gaza, Somalia, Mali), plus the exclusion of non-citizens from a welfare state whose benefits were never designed for them. Both of those mechanisms exist in Christian-majority countries too — in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in Haiti, in Guatemala, among migrant workers in the United States and in the Gulf of the Christian Atlantic. 7. The Christian-majority side of the same pattern To answer the question fairly, the comparison has to be run in both directions, with the same instruments. The least poverty ever measured is Christian-majority — and it is not charity Norway, Denmark, Finland and Iceland are Lutheran-majority societies with the lowest poverty rates in the historical record, and the mechanism is not religious: it is state capacity. They tax around half of national income, deliver universal services, insure wages, and let the state, not the family or the parish, absorb shocks. Across the OECD, public social spending averaged about 21 per cent of GDP in 2024 , with Austria, Finland and France above 30 per cent. This manual is built against both failure modes. Rule 01 Read, then run Every command is annotated with what it changes and how to undo it. If a line has no explanation, treat it as hostile — including lines in this manual. Rule 02 Verify, don't trust Checksums, signatures, systemctl status , pfctl -sr , packet captures. The properties, defined operationally Property Question it answers Typical control Typical failure Confidentiality Can someone read it? Disk encryption, TLS, access control Key stored on the same disk; screen unlocked Integrity Can someone change it? Signatures, Secure Boot, hashes, file integrity monitoring Unsigned updates, writable /boot Availability Can you still use it? Backups, redundant keys, recovery codes Lost LUKS header, forgotten passphrase, dead YubiKey Anonymity Can the action be tied to any identity? Worked example 1 — the developer with a day job Assets: source code, cloud credentials, personal email, home address. Adversary: A1/A2 for marketing data, A4 for credential stuffing and package-supply-chain attacks. Impact: account takeover, doxxing, employer breach. Budget: two evenings, no recurring cost. Worked example 2 — the journalist covering local government Assets: source identities, unpublished drafts, location patterns. Adversary: A3/A4 plus the possibility of A5 through legal orders. Adversary: A1 scanning bots and A4 credential stuffing; occasional physical access by guests. Impact: botnet enrollment, data loss. Resulting controls: key-only SSH, pf deny-by-default, jails for exposed services, automated encrypted backups, ZFS snapshots, and a router-level rule that exposes exactly one port. Do these before optimizing anything exotic. Universal wins, in order of return on effort # Control Why it is near-universal 1 Patch promptly Nearly all mass compromise uses known vulnerabilities. Foi, ao longo de toda a história recente, a presença policial nas grandes cidades — sobretudo Lisboa e Porto — ao contrário da GNR, que cobria o interior, as estradas e o litoral. Essa distinção não é apenas geográfica: é uma distinção de ritmo, de perfil e de pressão. Uma polícia de cidade vive o chão de rua, freguesia a freguesia, o trânsito, o mercado, a proximidade e o barulho de quem está sempre à porta. Durante o Estado Novo, a PSP, como todas as forças de segurança, funcionou dentro de uma ordem política autoritária. É uma parte da história que não se pode apagar nem glorificar demais: a instituição serviu o regime da mesma maneira que serviria a República depois, porque é uma instituição estrutural, não uma ideologia. Distinguir isso não é pedantismo; é o primeiro exercício de leitura honesta de qualquer dossiê sobre polícia. O dragão da GNR escreveu sobre essa linha antes, com um tom que não esconde a tensão: GNR — O Dragão que Guarda a Lei . 1832 A Guarda Nacional surge Nasce com a necessidade de organizar a segurança nas cidades e nos espaços de conflito do século XIX. O nome e a estrutura vão mudando, mas a função urbana deixa marcas. 1900s–1930s A PSP consolida-se A polícia de Lisboa e Porto ganha maior capacidade de intervenção urbana, com unidades que antes eram mais dispersas a tornarem-se instituições de presença constante. 1933–1974 Estado Novo A PSP funciona no quadro de uma ditadura. Não é só "força de ordem" — é uma instituição envolvida na vida política, com o dever de obediência e a margem que toda a polícia tem. Um dossiê honesto não esconde essa linha; ela é o pano de fundo das perguntas sobre coragem e sobre obediência. 1974 em diante A democracia republicana Após o 25 de Abril, a PSP passa a fazer parte de uma ordem democrática com novas regras, novas expectativas e novas tensões entre obediência, lei e intervenção. Uma das perguntas que atravessa o dossiê não é apenas histórica. É ética. Se a polícia acata ordens, até quando acata? Se acata sempre, até que ponto foi "força pública" em vez de "braço do poder"? O blog já escreveu sobre essa questão com outra inclinação, num tom que mistura sistema, ética e ironia: Discurso do Eterno Macaco às Forças de Segurança do Mundo . A leitura completa ajuda a entender que a PSP nunca é só um braço; às vezes é o reflexo de um país inteiro. 02 · SÍMBOLOS O Tigre: três línguas, um animal O Tigre da PSP não é um acidente gráfico. É um animal que carrega coragem, força e presença; é também um símbolo que, em Portugal e na Ásia, fala línguas muito diferentes. Por isso é normal que o mesmo símbolo soe diferente dependendo de quem o olha e de onde o olha. Daqui nasce uma das lições centrais deste artigo: o símbolo não é uma tradução, é um convite para ler o contexto. Em Portugal, o tigre evoca a proeza, a vigília, a rapidez, a força necessária para a rua e para a crise. Isso não significa que seja "o animal do mal" ou "o animal da barbárie"; é um animal que, no imaginário público, tende a oscilar entre força necessária e força excessiva. Nesta página, trabalhamos essa dualidade de forma intencional: o tigre como coragem, não como crueldade, e reconhecendo que a crueldade existe e que a coragem, quando se desvia da sua função, pode tornar-se violência. Na Ásia, o tigre carrega um peso muito mais antigo e muito mais aberto. É um dos animais mais importantes da cultura chinesa, coreana, japonesa e vietnamita. Não é o dragão, que é celestial e raramente visto de perto. É o tigre: terrestre, audacioso, protetor em muitos contextos, símbolo de homens corajosos em outros, presença de bravura em gestos que exigem coragem e não apenas força. Quando se diz que o tigre é símbolo dos homens corajosos na Ásia, não é uma frase decorativa; é uma observação de que a coragem, na Ásia, está ligada ao animal que enfrenta, protege, avança e, em muitas lendas, não recua. 03 · ÁSIA Na Ásia, o tigre dos homens corajosos A afirmação de que "na Ásia também o Tigre é símbolo dos homens corajosos" é mais profunda do que parece. Na cartografia cultural asiática o tigre é, frequentemente, o animal que liga o homem à sua coragem de forma mais direta do que o dragão. O dragão é, em grande parte da Ásia, o poder celestial, a sabedoria, a água e a chuva, o que unifica e o que governa. O tigre é o corpo que age. É o animal que corre, que protege o território, que enfrenta o perigo, que não representa apenas o poder do céu, mas a coragem de quem está em terra firme. Na China, o tigre é um dos quatro animais sagrados, ao lado do dragão azul, da ave vermelha (fénix) e da tartaruga negra. O tigre azul (青虎) pode aparecer em muitas variantes; em algumas tradições é protetor, noutras é o animal que combate a energia negativa. Há um detalhe surpreendente na leitura ocidental comum: o tigre asiático não é apenas "o animal feroz". É a força que o homem cultiva para estar à frente do perigo sem se deixar levar por ele. Essa é a coragem que interessa a este artigo: não a força que ataca, mas a coragem que enfrenta com responsabilidade. No Japão, o tigre aparece em mitologia, em trajes de teatro e em armaduras, como símbolo de proteção e bravura. Na Coreia, o tigre é, junto com o dragão, um dos dois animais que aparecem tanto na imagética protetora como na lenda. No Vietname, o tigre é fortemente associado à resistência e à coragem nacional. Em todas essas culturas, há uma linha comum: o tigre é usado para falar de homens que a exercem, não apenas de animais que fazem medo. Não é estranho, portanto, que uma polícia portuguesa use um tigre no seu emblema. O que é estranho — ou pelo menos controverso — é usar um símbolo associado à coragem e depois esquecer que a coragem exige limites. A diferença entre coragem e brutalidade é de intenção, de proporcionalidade, de cuidado com o inocente. Essa distinção é o trabalho central não só de um dossiê, mas de uma democracia que quer olhar para a sua polícia sem desviar os olhos nem usar a retórica para fechar os olhos. Comentário pedagógico — o símbolo como convite à introspecção O tigre da PSP não deve ser apenas uma imagem de força. Deve ser um lembrete de que a coragem de um homem está envolvida na coragem de um animal — a de avançar quando é necessário, a de recuar quando a lei e a dignidade exigem. Quando um símbolo de coragem é usado sem reflexão, corre-se o risco de transformar coragem em licença para hiper-reacção. Por isso, ler símbolos de força pública exige mais que admiração: exige a pergunta sobre os limites. Para aprofundar essa leitura, o blog deu já outros passos: Police Groups in Society — A Technical Manual , Police the Police e Human Rights Include You . Leitura externa: Wikipédia — Tigre e Wikipédia — The Four Symbols (tigre na Ásia) . 04 · ESTRUTURA O mapa das divisões atuais A PSP não funciona como um exército em campanha, mas como um conjunto de divisões, unidades e serviços urbanos, com jurisdição nas grandes cidades e nos espaços onde a presença policial é mais densa. A estrutura é uma das coisas que mais muda e mais se confunde; não é raro que o cidadão comum misture PSP, GNR, PJ e outras forças num só bloco. Este artigo tenta dar um panorama público e honesto sem descer ao nível de inventar dados que ninguém pode confirmar. Para ler a PSP é preciso ler, antes de tudo, a sua função básica: garantir a segurança pública nas zonas urbanas, prestar serviço de proximidade, fazer cumprir a lei, entrar em contextos de conflito, proteger pessoas e empresas e, em muitos casos, ser a face mais visível do Estado no dia a dia. Essa função é rodeada de pressões: trânsito, criminalidade de rua, conflitos sociais, tensões políticas, custos da mão de obra, desgaste dos agentes e confiança — ou desconfiança — do público. A PSP publica comunicados e relatórios setoriais, mas não um quadro aberto e comparável de tempos de resposta, queixas ou uso da força. python-cli: Monkey Blog · The Shell, Extended Home EN PT Terminal tools · a manual in nineteen parts The Shell, Extended Python's best software does not live in an app store. It lives in a terminal, in a repository with a README, behind one command that installs it. This manual is about that command: how to build a virtual environment, how to keep it out of the system, and thirty real GitHub projects worth the trouble — from posting to Mastodon to OCR on a scanned contract. Nineteen parts Thirty apps venv · pipx · uv Install builder Ten errors, solved Every repo linked I have never made a venv Part 02: seven commands, one afternoon, and nothing else on your machine changes. Show me the tools first Part 06: every tool with its package, version, home page and one-line purpose, plus the command for your machine. Just give me the command Part 03: one isolated environment per app, and no dependency conflicts. An install just failed Part 16: the ten messages that stop people, and the fix for each one. 01 Never install into the system Python Almost every broken Python install starts with one of two sentences: "it worked on my machine" and "I ran it with sudo". Both are the same mistake — installing a project's dependencies into the one interpreter your operating system uses to run itself. There is a rule that removes the whole class of problem, and it fits in three lines. One: the system Python belongs to the system Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, macOS and Arch all ship Python because parts of the operating system are written in it. Installing packages into it means two projects can demand two versions of the same library, and the loser is usually your desktop. Modern distributions now refuse: pip exits with error: externally-managed-environment , which is not a bug, it is a locked door with a reason. Two: a project gets a venv, an app gets pipx If you will import the thing from your own code, it belongs in a virtual environment inside the project folder. If you will only type its name at the prompt, it belongs in pipx (or uv), which gives the app its own private venv and puts a single launcher on your PATH. Nothing else on the machine sees it. Three: no sudo, ever, for pip The single exception is your distribution's package manager — apt install python3-venv , dnf install python3-pip — which installs the tooling, never a project's dependencies. If a README tells you to sudo pip install , the README is old; use the project's pyproject or the PyPI name with pipx. What that error actually says PEP 668 lets a distribution mark its interpreter as externally managed, with an EXTERNALLY-MANAGED marker file next to the standard library. pip reads it and stops. You can override it with --break-system-packages ; you should not, and no command in this manual needs it. The escape hatch is a venv, which is one command away. Three tools, three jobs Tool What it is for Use it when What it costs venv A folder with its own Python, its own pip and its own site-packages. Built into Python since 3.3. You are writing code that imports the library, or you need an exact pinned set of versions for one project. 20–200 MB per environment, and one activation command per terminal. pipx A manager of isolated environments, one per command-line app, with a launcher symlinked into ~/.local/bin . The package provides a command you run (yt-dlp, toot, csvkit) and you never import it. A few MB per app; the disk cost is the price of never having a dependency conflict again. uv A single fast binary that does venvs, pip installs, Python version downloads and tool installs — the same jobs, in seconds. You install tools often, or you are tired of waiting for a resolver. uvx also runs an app without installing it at all. One more binary to trust and to update; it is written in Rust, not Python. The whole idea, on one screen One environment per app, no activation needed, and the command is addressed by its full path. This is the pattern the rest of the manual refines; everything else is convenience built on top of it. python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/media ~/.venvs/media/bin/pip install --upgrade pip ~/.venvs/media/bin/pip install yt-dlp ~/.venvs/media/bin/yt-dlp --version Nothing was installed system-wide, nothing needs sudo, and deleting ~/.venvs/media removes every trace. The three drawbacks are that the path is long, that each app needs its own folder, and that you have to remember which folder holds what — which is exactly what pipx removes. 02 The virtual environment, from zero A venv is not a virtual machine and it is not magic: it is a directory containing a symlink to your Python, a copy of the launcher scripts, and a site-packages folder that pip writes into. Activating it changes one environment variable, PATH , so that python means this folder instead of the system one. That is the entire mechanism. Seven commands, in order Check what you have python3 --version should print 3.11 or newer for most of the apps in this manual (mitmproxy, for one, wants 3.12 — each project states its floor on PyPI). If the version is older than a project needs, install a newer interpreter next to the old one rather than replacing the system's. Install the venv module, if your distribution split it out Debian and Ubuntu ship Python without ensurepip , which makes python3 -m venv fail with "ensurepip is not available". One package fixes it permanently: sudo apt install python3-venv . Fedora and Arch already include it; macOS from python.org includes it; Homebrew's Python does too. Create it inside the project Name it .venv and put it in the project root — editors, linters and every tutorial already look there. The folder is disposable: no data lives in it, only symlinks and wheels. Activate it Activation is a convenience, not a requirement. It exists so that typing python and pip does the right thing; the environment works identically if you call .venv/bin/python directly, which is what cron jobs and scripts should do. Install with pip, then freeze Install what you need, confirm it imports, then write the exact versions to a file. pip freeze records everything including transitive dependencies; a hand-written requirements.txt records only your intent. For applications, freeze. For libraries, pin the direct dependencies and let the resolver work. Leave, and come back later deactivate restores the old PATH. Next session, activate again, or skip activation and use the full path. On a server, always skip it: a script that depends on an activated shell breaks the first time it runs from cron. Delete it when it rots When upgrades go wrong, the fastest fix is rm -rf .venv and create it again from requirements.txt . Ten seconds, no residue. This is the habit that makes the rest of this manual safe: environments are cheap, so never repair one for an hour. The same three commands on each system System Create Activate Leave Linux / macOS (bash, zsh) python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate deactivate fish python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate.fish deactivate Windows (PowerShell) py -m venv .venv .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 deactivate Windows (cmd) py -m venv .venv .venv\Scripts\activate.bat deactivate PowerShell blocks the activation script By default Windows refuses to run Activate.ps1 because it is an unsigned script. The fix is per-user, not per-machine: Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned . If you would rather not touch policy at all, call .venv\Scripts\python.exe directly and never activate. A real session, with the output it should give cd ~/projects/scrape python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip pip install requests beautifulsoup4 python -c "import requests, bs4; print(requests.__version__, bs4.__version__)" pip freeze > requirements.txt deactivate From another machine, or after deleting the folder: python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && pip install -r requirements.txt . That one line is the entire portability story of a Python project, and it is why requirements.txt is committed while .venv is not. What goes into git Commit requirements.txt (or pyproject.toml with a lock file). Never commit .venv : it contains absolute paths, platform-specific binaries and tens of megabytes. One line in .gitignore — .venv/ — prevents a hundred confusing clones. The two flags that cause trouble --system-site-packages lets an environment see the system's packages, which quietly reintroduces the conflict you were escaping. --without-pip creates an environment with no installer; you then need python -m ensurepip . Neither is needed for anything in this manual. 03 pipx: one command per app, no conflicts pipx is the answer to a specific question: what if I want the command, not the library? It creates a private venv for each app under ~/.local/pipx/venvs , installs the package there with the right interpreter, and symlinks only the launcher into ~/.local/bin . Two apps can then depend on two incompatible versions of the same library and neither notices the other exists. Start here # Debian / Ubuntu sudo apt install pipx # Fedora sudo dnf install pipx # macOS (Homebrew) brew install pipx # or, with any Python already installed python3 -m pip install --user pipx pipx ensurepath # open a new terminal, then pipx install toot toot --help ensurepath writes the PATH line in your shell's startup file. If the next shell still says command not found , the file was the wrong one — see part 05 — or the shell cached its command list and needs hash -r . The eight pipx commands worth memorising Command What it does Why you would type it pipx install NAME Creates a venv and links the launcher. The normal case. Add extras in quotes: pipx install "qrcode[pil]" . pipx list Shows every app, its version and its command names. When you cannot remember whether you already installed something. pipx upgrade NAME Upgrades that app only, in its own venv. yt-dlp and gallery-dl need this often: sites change weekly. pipx upgrade-all Upgrades every app pipx manages. A monthly habit, not a daily one. pipx uninstall NAME Removes the venv and the launcher. A clean removal with no leftovers in site-packages. pipx inject NAME PKG Adds a library to that app's venv. For plugins and optional backends, without touching other apps. pipx run NAME Runs the app in a temporary venv that is thrown away. Trying something once without committing to it. pipx reinstall NAME --python 3.12 Rebuilds that app's venv with another interpreter. When an app needs a newer (or older) Python than the default. The plugin pattern A command with an ecosystem — beets, llm, mkdocs — usually wants a plugin. Install the app, then pipx inject beets beets-fetchart . The plugin lands in the same private venv, so it cannot break any other tool, and pipx upgrade beets leaves it alone. Directory What lives there Should you touch it? ~/.local/bin Launchers from pipx and uv, plus any pip install --user script. No — but it must be on PATH. This is the directory ensurepath adds. ~/.local/pipx/venvs/<app> The private environment of each pipx app, with its dependencies. Never by hand. pipx owns it; edit through inject or reinstall. ~/.venvs Environments that belong to no project — a scratch toolbox of your own. Yes, freely. It is just folders you invented; delete them when bored. /usr/local/bin System-wide launchers, usually from your distribution or a make install. Only with sudo, and only for things the package manager did not provide. Adding it once, per shell # bash — ~/.bashrc zsh — ~/.zshrc export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" # fish fish_add_path ~/.local/bin # then, in the current shell source ~/.bashrc command -v toot On Windows the equivalent is setx PATH "%PATH%;%USERPROFILE%\AppData\Roaming\Python\Scripts" in a fresh cmd, and a restart of the terminal. Get the order right and everything else composes. 1. PATH: the only config most people need Programs are found through PATH , left to right. Console scripts installed with pip --user and pipx land in ~/.local/bin (Linux/macOS) or %APPDATA%\Python\Python3xx\Scripts (Windows). If that directory is missing from PATH , the install succeeds and the command "does not exist". bash · make user scripts visible (Linux/macOS) copy echo "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n' | grep -E '\.local/bin|\.venv|pyenv' # Append once, in ~/.profile for POSIX shells, or ~/.zshrc / ~/.bashrc for interactive shells: echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.profile exec "$SHELL" -l command -v pytest ruff uv pipx Which file: .bashrc, .profile, .zshrc? ~/.bashrc runs for interactive non-login shells; ~/.profile runs for login shells (and is read by most display managers); zsh uses ~/.zshrc + ~/.zprofile . GUI applications and systemd services often start without your interactive shell config, so a PATH that works in the terminal can still be missing under systemd. That is why services should call interpreters by absolute path (see Level 13), not rely on PATH . Bad decision — alias python=python3 and alias pip=pip3 It feels harmless. It is not: aliases do not apply to scripts, cron, systemd, IDEs, or subprocess , so you get a machine that behaves one way interactively and another way in production. On Debian/Ubuntu, python is deliberately absent from the base system because Python 2-era tooling would silently pick it up. Worse, alias pip=pip3 hides which interpreter pip belongs to. The robust fix is to create a virtual environment and let python and pip both resolve inside .venv/bin . If you truly need a user-level python , use a symlink in ~/.local/bin pointing at a specific version and understand that every non-shell context will ignore it. 2. pip: configure it once, correctly pip reads configuration from three scopes — global ( /etc/pip.conf ), user ( ~/.config/pip/pip.conf ), and site ( .venv/pip.conf ) — plus PIP_* environment variables. Later scopes win, and command-line flags beat everything. Inspect before editing: bash · pip configuration copy python3 -m pip config debug # every file considered, and its values python3 -m pip config list python3 -m pip --version # confirm which pip, from which environment python3 -m pip cache dir # where wheels are cached ini · ~/.config/pip/pip.conf copy [global] # Only change these if your organisation actually runs a mirror. # index-url = https://pypi.org/simple timeout = 20 retries = 3 disable-pip-version-check = true [install] # Fail loudly instead of silently drifting when a version is yanked. prefer-binary = true Bad decision — trusted-host as a permanent fix Adding trusted-host or --trusted-host disables TLS certificate verification for that index. People add it to silence corporate-proxy errors and then forget it exists; every package they install afterwards is trivially interceptable. The correct fixes are: install your organisation's CA certificate into the system trust store, point pip at it with cert = /path/ca.pem , or configure the proxy in pip.conf . If you inherit a machine with trusted-host set, treat it as a security finding. 3. The environment variables that matter Python honours a set of PYTHON* variables at startup. A few are useful; several are dangerous because they change behaviour for every program you run. Use python -X option or -E / -I in scripts to ignore the environment entirely. Selected PYTHON* environment variables Variable Effect Verdict PYTHONPATH Prepends directories to sys.path . Avoid. Shadowing risk; use installed packages or uv run . PYTHONSTARTUP Script executed by the interactive interpreter only. Safe for conveniences, never for application logic. PYTHONDEVMODE Enables development mode: extra warnings, debug hooks. Good in CI ( PYTHONDEVMODE=1 ). PYTHONWARNINGS Warning filters, e.g. error to turn warnings into exceptions. Useful in tests; do not rely on it in production. PYTHONSAFEPATH Like -P : do not prepend the script's directory / CWD. Good hardening for tools run on untrusted trees. PYTHONNOUSERSITE Ignores

racismo: O Racismo é mais do que Palavras Comparativas Ser "Preto" é ser objectivado e limitado a uma cor só, sem forma, sem irregularidades da cor, tão ou mais escura do que a cor da sombra de um objecto estático ou em movimento ou até, um ser que está parado ou em movimento. Ser "preto" poderá ser ofensivo nessa noção de que só a cor preta é preta e ser "preto" é ser cor sem incluir a forma. Ser "branco" é igual e ser "amarelo" também. É limitar e simplificar o Ser a algo tão básico quanto uma cor. Mas o Racismo não é uma comparação, pois as comparações servem a simplificação das objectivações. Um Leão é um animal selvagem e quando alguém diz que outra pessoa parece "um leão", estará também a fazer uma comparação irreal e falsa, pois há vários aspectos físicos e comportamentais que se diferenciam entre um leão e uma pessoa. O mesmo acontece com a expressão que define uma pessoa de "Macaco". Existe um programa na Internet (no YouTube) chamado "O Lado Negro da Força", que se dedica não só a falar da cultura Africana, mas também a referir e a discutir problemas associados ao Racismo, sendo que a pessoa que lidera o programa, tenta fazer a relação entre a expressão de "macaco" com racismo, por causa de uma espécie de semelhança visual, que é bem irreal, sendo que os considerados agressores da história, usavam esta expressão para definir pessoas de origem africana, ficando assim na memória das pessoas africanas, como uma expressão que representa Racismo. A meu ver, este tipo de relação deveria ser combatida via a vontade de vencer e não deveria ser alimentada, via a vontade de ser vítima do que é puramente subjectivo. Nenhuma pessoa é mais do que uma pessoa e caso uma qualquer comparação tente definir uma pessoa como algo mais além de ser uma pessoa, essa definição será falsa, ou poderá ser unicamente subjectiva e criativa. Mesmo entendendo o sofrimento de quem foi alvo da expressão que ofende, deverei lembrar o poder da mente, que tem a capacidade de negar o Verbo ou até dar-lhe um novo sentido e signficado. Nasci numa cultura que usa comparações desde sempre e mesmo que essa técnica tenha sido combatida e objectivada como a origem do " Bulling ", a meu ver, mesmo tendo sido vítima dessa técnica, não é "bulling" nem creio que a técnica seja ofensiva, mas verdadeiramente educativa. O Racismo é um comportamento físico que ataca fisicamente alguém, independentemente da sua origem ou cor, aplicando punições físicas e nada subjectivas (tal como as usadas pela língua em forma de comparações), tal como o uso da Violência Física. Se as palavras magoam, significa que somos capazes de pensar, pois até as palavras que não focam o nosso ser, podem produzir dor, tal como ver injustiças que outras pessoas são alvo. Por exemplo, actualmente quando vejo notícias de padres que violam crianças ou que declaram afirmações tais como "mais vale violar uma criança do que usar técnicas de masturbação", produz em mim uma dor e tanto faz qual a cor ora do padre ora da criança. São os Reis da Selva é o que alguns acreditam e por isso, os Reis tornaram-se seres impiedosos e injustos. recycling: Monkey Blog · Second Lives Home EN PT Second lives · a manual in seventeen parts Nothing Is Garbage A bin is a decision someone else already made for you. This manual takes it back: what kitchen scraps, garden clippings, old clothes, jars, tins, pallets and dead electronics can become instead — with the recipes, the numbers, the traps and the sources, for a household, a garden, or a small business. Seventeen parts 75+ second lives Bin audit Compost calculator From waste to income Sources Start with my own bin Part 03: one week, a kitchen scale, and a number instead of a feeling. I want to use the scraps tonight Part 04: five things to do with peels, stale bread and coffee before they become a smell. I have a garden and a compost problem Part 05: the carbon/nitrogen balance, with a calculator that says how many litres to add. I want this to pay Part 13: repair, upcycling, compost and workshops — what people actually charge for. 01 The rule that changes everything Waste is not a property of an object. It is the moment someone stops imagining a use for it. That is good news, because imagination is cheap — and the order in which you apply it decides whether you are solving a problem or just moving it. Refuse — the only free option The bag, the straw, the second plastic tray, the free T-shirt at an event. Every object refused costs nothing to store, sort, clean or feel guilty about. This is the only rung with no downstream work. Reduce — use less of it, for longer A bigger jar of yoghurt, a refill bottle, a repair instead of a replacement. Reduction is boring and it is where most of the kilos actually disappear. Reuse and repair — the interesting middle Jars, crates, clothes, furniture, electronics. This manual lives here: the second life that keeps the material in service without melting it down. Rot — let biology do the work Food scraps and garden clippings are not waste, they are next year's soil. Composting is the cheapest transformation available to a household, and the one most often skipped. Recycle — the last resort that looks like the first Recycling destroys the object to recover the material. It needs energy, clean streams and a market. It is good, and it is fourth best — which is why a page about it should not start there. What you gain Money that stays in the house: a jar, a crate and a repaired lamp are things you no longer buy. Better bins: less smell, fewer flies, no liquid at the bottom, half the volume. Skills that transfer — cutting, sewing, composting, wiring a plug are the same skills at 60 as at 6. A garden that feeds itself instead of importing bags of soil. A reason to know your neighbours: the person with pallets, the café with buckets, the man who fixes toasters. What it costs Time, and the honest admission that ten minutes of labour can be worth less than a €2 object. Storage: the fatal temptation is a garage full of "someday". Every project needs a deadline or it is hoarding with better vocabulary. Standards: some second lives are not safe — food contact, children's toys, electrical work, anything structural. Aesthetic risk: visible mending is beautiful, a shelf made of three different woods is a shelf. The uncomfortable part: recycling is an industry with losses, and much of what you sort is burned or shipped. The scale, in four numbers. The average person in the EU generated 517 kg of municipal waste in 2024, and 48 % of it was recycled or composted. Biowaste is the single largest fraction of that bin at 28.8 % — food and garden waste, the part a household can transform without any industry at all. Globally, 1.05 billion tonnes of food were wasted in 2022, about 19 % of everything available to consumers, and food loss and waste produce 8–10 % of greenhouse-gas emissions. You cannot compost your way out of a supply chain. You can, however, remove a third of your own bin and half its smell this month. 02 Read the bin: eight materials, eight futures Every object is a material wearing a shape. Identify the material and the options appear — and so do the exclusions, which matter more. What each family wants to become, and where the second life stops being a good idea Family Typical pieces Best second life Where it stops The three questions before you keep anything A house is not a warehouse. Answer all three out loud, because a "maybe" is a no. Do I have a use, today? Not a use in the abstract: this shelf, this window, this person's birthday. Do I have the other half? A jar without a lid, a lamp without a cable, a frame without glass — the missing part is the project. Is it safe for that use? Food, children, heat, electricity and load-bearing are the five things you cannot improvise. 03 Audit your own bin Guilt is a bad measuring instrument. One week, one kitchen scale, five numbers — and you will know exactly which habit is worth changing, instead of changing all of them badly. People in the household Food and garden waste (kg per week) Plastic and metal packaging (kg per week) Paper and cardboard (kg per week) Glass (kg per week) Textiles and other (kg per week) Total / week — Per person / year — Could rot — Could be recycled — Still mixed — How to read the result The EU average is 517 kg per person per year. Under 300 means you are already unusual; over 600 means volume, not guilt, is the place to start. But the number that matters is the third one: the organic share is the only stream a household can process at home, without markets, trucks or a single kilowatt-hour. if organic wins Build the compost, then the garden A balcony bokashi bin handles 15 litres a month and takes no space. A worm bin handles a family's peels, and gives back the only fertiliser you will need for pots. if packaging wins Change the shop, not the bin Packaging is decided at the shelf. Two refill stops, one bigger format and a market with loose produce do more than a year of folding cartons perfectly. if textiles win Open a repair basket A box with needle, thread, patches and a spare button turns "I have nothing to wear" into twenty minutes. The rest becomes rags, then wicks, then compost-adjacent dust. 04 The kitchen: five lives before the bin A kitchen throws away food, water and packaging in the same gesture. These five habits catch the first two, cost nothing, and are the ones people keep doing after the novelty wears off. 20 minutes + 2 weeks · €0 Citrus-peel vinegar cleaner The peels you were going to bin become a degreaser strong enough for the stove. Peels of 3–4 oranges, lemons or limes 1 L of white vinegar (the cheap one) A jar with a lid Pack the peels into the jar and cover with vinegar. Leave it two weeks in a cupboard, shaking when you remember. Strain, keep the liquid, dilute half and half with water for surfaces. Never on marble, limestone or unsealed stone — the acid eats the surface. Never mixed with bleach. 5 minutes · 1–3 weeks Regrow from the end Spring onion, leek, celery, lettuce hearts and carrot tops will push new leaves from a centimetre of water. The root end, 2–3 cm, still attached A shallow glass or a saucer Light, but not direct summer sun Stand the end in 1 cm of water, cut side up. Change the water every day — stagnant water is what rots it. Cut what you need, twice at most, then give the rest to the compost. The second growth is thinner and less flavoured: this is a pleasure, not a food supply. 40 minutes · freezer Scrap stock Onion skins, carrot peel, celery leaves, herb stems, a parmesan rind: a litre of stock from what was already in the bin. A bag of peels kept in the freezer until it is full Cold water to cover, a bay leaf, ten peppercorns Salt, added only at the end Cover the scraps with cold water and bring to a bare simmer. Thirty to forty minutes, never a hard boil — boiling makes it cloudy and bitter. Strain, salt, cool fast, freeze in jars with 2 cm of headspace. No mouldy scraps, no potato leaves or green sprouts (solanine), no cabbage in quantity. Four days in the fridge, three months frozen. 10 minutes · 150 °C Stale bread, three ways Bread does not go off, it goes hard — and hard bread is an ingredient. Croutons: cubes, oil, salt, 15 minutes at 150 °C Pangrattato: blitz with garlic and parsley, toast in a pan Breadcrumbs: blitz dry and freeze in a bag Cut or tear before it turns to stone; a dry loaf grates into crumbs in a minute. Dry it fully before storing, or the bag grows mould. Mould is not a crust problem: the toxins survive toasting. Mouldy bread goes to the compost, never to the oven. 0 minutes · daily Coffee grounds A café gives away kilos of them. They are a green compost input, a mild abrasive and a deodoriser — in that order of usefulness. Compost: a thin layer, never a solid cake — they mat and go anaerobic Scrub: with oil and sugar, for hands and sinks Fridge: a cup in the door absorbs smells for a week Skip the old myth about acid-loving plants: spent grounds are nearly neutral. Do not dump them down the sink. Food safety, in one line each. Cool leftovers fast and shallow. Reheat once. Anything mouldy goes to compost, not to "cut off the bad bit". Rice, pasta and reheated meat are the usual suspects, not the leftovers you can smell. 05 The garden: compost is chemistry with a smell Composting fails for one of three reasons: too wet, too dry, or the wrong balance of carbon to nitrogen. The first two are visible. The third is the one this calculator fixes. Greens, by volume (litres) Browns, by volume (litres) Browns : greens — Add — The target is about 25–30 parts carbon to one part nitrogen, which in practice is two to three volumes of browns for one of greens. Greens are wet and Nitrogen-rich: peels, coffee, grass, fresh leaves. Browns are dry and Carbon-rich: cardboard, egg boxes, dry leaves, straw, sawdust from untreated wood, toilet-roll tubes. fast Hot compost, one cubic metre Build the pile in one go, three parts browns to one of greens, damp as a wrung sponge. It reaches 55–65 °C in three days; turn it when it cools, and it is finished in six to ten weeks. small space Bokashi, on a balcony A sealed bucket with bran inoculated with lactic bacteria ferments everything, including fish and cheese, in two weeks. It is not compost: bury the result 20 cm deep, or feed it to a worm bin. with worms Worm bin, indoors A plastic box, shredded cardboard, a handful of composting worms, and peels buried under the bedding. No smell when it is balanced; citrus, onion and cooked food in quantity upset it. What never goes in a home compost: meat, fish and dairy in an open pile (bokashi is the exception), pet faeces, glossy or thermal paper, treated wood, "compostable" plastic unless your council accepts it, and anything that has been in contact with pesticide. A compost heap is not a furnace: it does not sterilise. The free soil amendments you already own Leaf mould is the slowest and best thing in this section: a wire ring, wet leaves, a year, and you have a seed-sowing compost that costs nothing. Eggshells need crushing and years to break down — they are a slow calcium bank, not a quick fix. Wood ash is potash, useful in small amounts on soil, never on blueberries or acid-lovers, and never from painted or treated wood. 06 Water, used twice A litre that has washed a vegetable is not dirty, it is displaced. The trick is to move it once, by hand or by gravity, and to know what must not go with it. garden Greywater to a mulch basin Bath or shower water, still warm, poured into a shallow basin dug around a tree and covered with wood chips. The soil filters it; the plant drinks it. No tank, no pump, no smell. kitchen Vegetable washing water The bowl you rinsed the lettuce in goes on the houseplants or the balcony pots. One bowl a day is 100 litres a year that never reaches the drain. cooking Pasta, rice and egg water Cooled, unsalted cooking water carries starch that feeds soil life. Salted water goes to the drain, not the pots — a few years of it turns a pot salty. free Air-conditioner condensate A split unit in a Portuguese summer makes litres a day at almost zero conductivity. Perfect for the garden, not for drinking, and not for misting anything you breathe near. Greywater rules that are not negotiable: No kitchen sink water with grease, no dishwasher water, no water from nappies or toilets. No bleach, borax or fabric softener — they kill the soil you are trying to feed. Use it the same day, below the surface, and never on leaves you will eat raw. Not on root vegetables, not on seedlings, not in a drip system that will clog with soap. 07 Textiles: repair first, then remake Clothes are the most emotionally loaded object in the bin. They are also the easiest to keep: a needle, a patch and twenty minutes restore most of what people throw away. Less than 1 % of the material used to make clothes is recycled into new clothes, so the second life you give a shirt is not a small thing. 20 minutes · €0 The repair basket One box by the sofa turns mending from a project into a habit. Needles, two threads (dark and light), small scissors A tin of spare buttons, saved from old shirts Iron-on patches, or denim offcuts for knee repairs Mend while the hole is small: a stitch now, a replacement later. Reinforce the corners of a pocket with a triangle of stitches before they tear. Visible mending is a style, not a confession — sashiko lines look deliberate because they are. 15 minutes · no sewing The T-shirt bag A single shirt becomes a strong, washable bag for the market. One old T-shirt, the thicker the better Scissors Cut off the sleeves and widen the neck into handles. Cut a fringe along the hem, 8 cm deep, front and back. Tie each front fringe to the matching back fringe, two knots, and pull tight. It holds 5 kg of shopping. It does not hold glass bottles without a lining. a weekend · a craft The rag rug Every torn sheet and worn shirt becomes weft. The Portuguese version — trapos — is older than the recycling bin. Old fabric cut into 3 cm strips A hessian sack or a cheap rug base A crochet hook or a prodding tool Work from the centre out, rows 3 cm apart, pushing each strip through and knotting it. Mix colours deliberately: two tones of the same family read as a design. Use cotton and linen; synthetic fleece sheds fibres every wash and does not felt. When a textile is truly finished: cut it into rags first (kitchen, workshop, paint), then use the rags as plant ties or wicks, then take what is left to a textile bank — not the paper bin. Never put textiles in a home compost unless they are pure wool or cotton cut into small pieces; a polyester label will still be there in a decade. 08 Paper and cardboard: the quiet material Cardboard is the most useful free material in a city and the least respected. It is a carbon source for compost, a weed barrier, a seed pot, a firelighter and a prototype — and it is recyclable at the end of all of that. propagation Seed pots from tubes Toilet-roll tubes and newspaper rolls make deep pots for beans, sweet peas and tomatoes, which hate root disturbance. Plant the whole tube: it rots in the soil. weed control Sheet mulch Plain brown cardboard, tape and staples removed, overlapped 15 cm, wetted, covered with 10 cm of wood chips or compost. It smothers grass in a season and feeds worms underneath. fire Fire starters Rolls stuffed with shredded paper and dipped in melted candle ends. One per fire, and the firelighters you stop buying are €3 a box. office Notebooks from misprints Print on one side only and the other side becomes a notebook: fold, staple at the spine, cut the edges. A5 from A4, sixty pages, ten minutes. Paper that must not be composted or mulched: thermal receipts (they are coated and often contain bisphenols), glossy magazines, pizza boxes soaked in grease, anything with plastic tape or laminate, and shredded paper from an office with a confidential-waste contract. Plain brown card, newspaper and office paper are fine. 09 Glass and metal: containers that outlive us Glass is endlessly recyclable and effectively eternal in a cupboard. Metal is the same, with sharper edges. Both reward a little patience and punish improvisation around food and heat. pantry Jars that match their lids A shelf of identical jars with matching lids is better storage than anything you can buy: visible, airtight, stackable. Collect one brand's jars until the lids all fit, then stop collecting. light The jar lantern A clean jar, a length of copper wire as a handle, a candle stub or a solar garden light inside. Twenty minutes, and it is the best-looking thing on a summer table. garden Tin-can planters A large tin, holes punched in the base with a nail, a coat of paint outside: herbs on a wall. Rust is the only maintenance, and herbs do not mind it. protection Bottle cloches The bottom half of a plastic bottle over a seedling is a mini greenhouse for €0. Lift it by day or the plant cooks; the cap off means ventilation. Sharp things, honestly: Cut glass with a proper cutter, oil, and gloves; fire-polish edges or sand them wet. A cut bottle is a blade. Tin cans: file the inside rim, and never use a can that held paint or chemicals for food or for a planter with edible roots. Do not store acidic food in a rusty can or in aluminium that has been cut. Glass is for food; metal is for tools, planters and light. Aerosol cans, gas cartridges and batteries are not craft material. They go to the ecocentro, closed. 10 Wood and furniture: the strong second life Wood is the one material where salvage beats buying on quality, not just on principle. Old pine from a drawer bottom is denser and drier than anything in a DIY shed. structure The pallet bench One pallet, four castors, a cushion: a bench for a balcony in an afternoon. Sand the top, oil it, and check every board for cracks before it takes weight. storage Crates as shelving Wine and fruit crates stack into a shelf that needs no tools, moves with you and can go back to the market. Fix them to the wall if children are in the house. garden Drawers as planters A drawer with holes drilled in the base, lined with cardboard and filled with compost, is a salad bed for a wall or a windowsill. It lasts two or three seasons. repair The wobbly chair Ninety per cent of wobbles are a loose joint: clean the old glue with a knife, warm the joint, add wood glue and clamp for a day. Stronger than new, and free. The wood you must not take: Pallets stamped MB (methyl bromide, a fumigant) — take only HT, heat-treated. The stamp is on the block, not the board. Painted or varnished wood of unknown age: old paint can carry lead. Sanding it is the risk, not keeping it. Railway sleepers, telegraph poles and anything green-tinted from pressure treatment — creosote and arsenic salts do not belong near food or compost. MDF and chipboard that has been wet: it crumbles and the dust is not worth breathing. 11 Electronics: the box you must not open The most valuable waste in your house is also the most dangerous. E-waste contains copper, gold, aluminium and cobalt — and capacitors that hold a lethal charge long after the plug is out. The second life of a device is repair, resale, or a certified recycler. Not a screwdriver and a YouTube video, unless you know which part is which. 62 million tonnes. That is the world's e-waste in 2022, growing five times faster than the recycling that is documented — only about a fifth is formally collected and recycled. A phone in a drawer is not "saved"; it is a mine that has not been opened yet. first Repair before replacement A repair café is the cheapest technician in Europe: volunteers, tools, coffee, and a good chance the toaster only needs a €2 switch. Thousands of them exist; the map is the first link in the sources. cables The cable cull Every house has a bag of chargers for devices it no longer owns. An automated grader inspects the state of the system afterwards: does the user exist, is the volume mounted at boot, does the service answer on the port, is the firewall rule permanent. In many Red Hat exams your work is evaluated as a snapshot at the end, so a task you “did” with a command that did not persist is simply a task you did not do. The single most expensive sentence in the exam room “It works right now.” The grader is not watching you type. It evaluates the machine after you leave — often after a reboot. If your change lives only in the running kernel, the running firewalld, or a login shell’s environment, the grader sees nothing. Always test the reboot. The commonly cited threshold is 210/300 (70%); treat it as a planning heuristic, not a contract. How the scoring really behaves Tasks are weighted. Some are worth a handful of points, some a couple of dozen. That produces three non-obvious consequences: Partial credit exists, but only for finished sub-states. Half a RAID array scores nothing; a correct user account with a wrong supplementary group may still score the account. A broken system can zero adjacent tasks. If you disable SELinux to make httpd work, you have traded one task for three. If you corrupt /etc/fstab , the machine may not boot and every later task is unreachable. Finishing is a strategy. Nine complete tasks beat six perfect ones and four unfinished experiments. The exam rewards triage. What the exam room is actually like No internet. Red Hat’s lab environments normally have local repositories instead of the CDN. If you have only ever installed packages from the public internet, practise with a local repo. Documentation is usually available. man and info pages are part of the operating system, so man firewall-cmd is a legitimate research tool. --help is too. A search engine is not. Remote delivery is proctored. Webcam, microphone, a cleared desk, no second monitor, no phone. Read the environment requirements before exam day, not at 08:55. You may get a free retake on a failed first individual-exam attempt, subject to Red Hat’s current policy. Plan as if you will not. Certifications last three years. Renewal is by retaking the highest exam, passing another exam at the same level, or advancing a level — check the current FAQ for your specific credential. Bad decision #1 — studying by watching Watching a four-hour video course produces the feeling of competence without the recall. The exam requires you to type a correct, persistent configuration from a cold start while a clock runs. The only practice that transfers is breaking your own lab and fixing it . Every level in this manual therefore ends with commands you must run, not concepts you must recognise. Bad decision #2 — memorising the flag, not the model An administrator who memorised firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http but not why --permanent exists will forget --reload and score zero. Learn the model — runtime versus permanent, desired state versus current state — and the flags become predictable. This is the difference between an operator and a certificate holder. The exam does not ask whether you have seen the command. It asks whether the machine, tomorrow morning, still agrees with what you intended today. Pass the previous checkpoint to open it. 01 The shell as an instrument Files, streams, permissions, and the three seconds before you press Enter. Every later level assumes fluency here. Not “I can cd ” — fluency means you can answer “where did that output go?”, “why can’t this process read that file?”, and “what will this command do to the other eleven files matching the glob?” before you run it. EX200 begins with an essential tools domain that is deceptively small: redirection, grep , regex, SSH, archives, links, permissions, documentation. Those objectives are worth roughly a fifth of the exam, and they are the ones people lose points on because they stopped thinking about them years ago. Streams: the plumbing you cannot skip A process gets three file descriptors. Standard input (0) is what it reads, standard output (1) is what it prints, standard error (2) is where it complains. Redirection is just reassigning descriptors, and the shell applies it before the command runs. streams.sh shell copy # Send stdout to a file, truncating it $ ls -l /etc > /tmp/etc.txt # Append instead of truncate $ ls -l /var/log >> /tmp/etc.txt # Capture BOTH streams into one file (order matters) $ dnf install httpd > /tmp/install.log 2>&1 # Discard noise, keep the signal $ find / -name "*.conf" 2>/dev/null | wc -l # Feed a file as stdin $ sort < /etc/passwd # Here-document: multi-line stdin inside a script $ cat <<'EOF' > /tmp/motd Welcome to rhel.lab.example.com Authorised use only. EOF The classic order mistake 2>&1 > file and > file 2>&1 are not the same. In the first, stderr is pointed at the terminal (stdout’s current target) and then stdout is moved to the file, so errors still hit your screen. In the second, stdout goes to the file first and stderr is then duplicated onto it. Only the second captures both. Redirections are evaluated left to right, like assignments. Text surgery: grep, cut, sed, awk You do not need to be a regex wizard to pass. You need four tools and the confidence to combine them. Daily text tools Command Does Real invocation grep -Ei Line filter; -E extended regex, -i ignore case, -r recursive, -n line numbers, -v invert grep -Ein '^PermitRootLogin' /etc/ssh/sshd_config sed -i Stream edit in place; s/old/new/g sed -i 's/^SELINUX=.*/SELINUX=enforcing/' /etc/selinux/config awk Field-aware processing; default separator is whitespace, -F: for passwd awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 {print $1, $3}' /etc/passwd cut Column extraction by delimiter cut -d: -f1,7 /etc/passwd sort | uniq -c | sort -rn The frequency pipeline: count repeats, biggest first awk '{print $1}' /var/log/secure | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head regex-cheatsheet BRE / ERE copy # Anchors and classes — the 90% you actually use ^ start of line $ end of line . any single character .* any run of characters (greedy) [abc] one of a, b, c [^abc] anything except [a-z0-9] ranges \b word boundary (GNU) \{2,4\} repeat count in BRE; {2,4} in ERE with -E ( | ) alternation in ERE only # Find every commented or uncommented sshd setting that is not the default $ grep -E '^[[:space:]]*#?[[:space:]]*PasswordAuthentication' /etc/ssh/sshd_config Permissions: the model, then the syntax Mode bits are an octal triplet per class: owner, group, others. rwx is 4+2+1, so 750 means owner rwx, group r-x, others nothing. Two extra concepts decide most exam tasks: umask (default mode is 666 & ~umask for files, 777 & ~umask for directories) and the special bits . Special bits that appear in real incident reports Bit Octal Effect Legitimate use setuid 4000 Runs with the file owner’s UID passwd , su , mount — root-owned, tiny, audited setgid 2000 File: runs with group. Directory: new files inherit the directory’s group Shared team directories — the correct fix for “my colleague can’t edit it” sticky 1000 Only the owner may delete their file in a shared directory /tmp , /var/tmp permissions.sh shell copy # Symbolic and octal are equally valid on the exam # chmod u=rw,g=r,o= /etc/motd # chmod 640 /etc/motd # Recursive ownership, then verify # chown -R apache:apache /var/www/html # ls -ld /var/www/html # Shared directory: setgid + sticky, group-writable, no world access # mkdir -p /srv/shared # chgrp devs /srv/shared # chmod 2770 /srv/shared # Find everything world-writable outside volatile dirs — an audit staple # find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 ! -path '/tmp/*' ! -path '/var/tmp/*' -ls 2>/dev/null # Find SUID binaries (an attacker's shopping list) # find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f -exec ls -l {} \; 2>/dev/null Bad decision #3 — chmod -R 777 to “fix” a permission problem It works, in the same way that removing the front door fixes a broken lock. World-writable web content lets any local user — including a compromised service account — replace your PHP or your static assets, and it usually breaks SELinux expectations at the same time. It also hides the real cause, which is almost always one of: wrong owner, wrong group, missing traverse ( x ) permission on a parent directory, or a bad umask. Diagnose with namei -l /var/www/html/index.php , which prints the effective permissions of every path component. Then fix the one that is wrong. Links: two different objects A hard link is a second name for the same inode. It cannot cross filesystems and cannot point at a directory. A soft (symbolic) link is a tiny file containing a path; it can cross filesystems, can dangle, and can point at directories — which is why every service configuration in /etc that “just points somewhere” is a symlink. links.sh shell copy # ln /etc/hosts /root/hosts-hard # same inode, survives deleting the original name # ln -s /opt/app/current/release.conf /etc/app.conf # Prove the difference $ stat -c '%i %h %n' /etc/hosts /root/hosts-hard $ ls -li /etc/app.conf # A dangling symlink is not an error to the filesystem, only to the app $ readlink -f /etc/app.conf Finding things, archiving things find-and-tar.sh shell copy # find is a query language: path, test, action # find /etc -type f -name '*.conf' -newermt '-7 days' -printf '%TY-%Tm-%Td %p\n' | sort # find /var/log -type f -size +50M -exec ls -lh {} + # find /srv -type d -name cache -prune -o -type f -name '*.log' -print # Archives: c=create x=extract t=list f=file z=gzip J=xz j=bzip2 v=verbose # tar -czf /var/tmp/etc-$(date +%F).tar.gz /etc # tar -tzf /var/tmp/etc-2026-10-20.tar.gz | head # tar -xzf /var/tmp/etc-2026-10-20.tar.gz -C /root/restore # Preserve SELinux labels and ownership when archiving a whole tree # tar --selinux -cpzf /var/tmp/srv.tar.gz /srv # restorecon -Rv /srv Exam habit: verify, do not assume After every archive or mount task, list the contents or read the mount table. tar -tzf before you delete the source; findmnt /data after you mount it; ss -tlnp after you start a service. Verification is not extra credit — it is how you find out you scored zero while there is still time to fix it. Documentation: the only offline search engine you get man.sh shell copy $ man 5 passwd # section 5 = file formats $ man 8 mount # section 8 = admin commands $ man -k selinux # same as apropos: search descriptions $ mandb # rebuild the index if man -k finds nothing $ rpm -qd httpd # list docs shipped by a package $ ls /usr/share/doc/httpd/ Useful habit Inside man : / searches forward, n jumps to the next hit, G goes to the end (where EXAMPLES and SEE ALSO live), q quits.
